title: Nebraska’s 2023-2024 team compared to the last decade
text:
After years of near-misses and rebuilding, the 2023-2024 Nebraska Men’s Basketball team finally broke through, securing a coveted spot in the NCAA March Madness tournament. But where does this squad truly rank among its recent seasons? This analysis dives deep into the metrics of the last ten seasons of Nebraska Basketball before that season (so it will be 13 seasons total). I compared key performance indicators including win/loss ratio, Strength of Schedule , Points Per Game, and Opponent Points Per Game to determine the true quality of the 2023-2024 team. Through a combination of visualizations, I aim to deliver a clear, data-driven answer to the question: How good was the 2023-2024 team compared to the last decade?


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

Nebraska_Season <-read_csv("data/NCAA.csv")


ggplot(Nebraska_Season, aes(x = Season)) +
  
  # Overall Win %
  geom_line(aes(y = Overall_WinPct, group = 1),
            color = "lightblue", size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(y = Overall_WinPct), color = "black", size = 2.5) +
  geom_text(
  data = subset(Nebraska_Season, Season == "2023-24"),
  aes(
    x = Season,
    y = Overall_WinPct,
    label = "March Madness Team"
  ),
  vjust = -1,
  fontface = "italic",
  size = 3
) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1))+ 
  
  # Conference Win %
  geom_line(aes(y = Conf_WinPct, group = 1),
            color = "red", size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(y = Conf_WinPct), color = "black", size = 2.5) +
  
  labs(
    title = "How Nebraska’s Win Rates Have Evolved Over the Past Decade",
    subtitle = "Win percentage trends across conference and overall competition",
    caption = "By: Alex Zetterman | Source: Sports-Reference",
    x = "Season",
    y = "Win Percentage"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 0),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )









The line chart shows how Nebraska’s overall and conference win percentages have shifted over the past decade, highlighting periods of growth, inconsistency, and eventual stabilization. Both trend lines reveal that while Nebraska experienced several up-and-down seasons, the program has gradually strengthened its performance, especially in recent years. Ever since Fred Hoiberg took over in 2019 the success has gone up every season. The 2023–24 season labeled “March Madness Team” marks one of the highest combined win rates in the dataset, indicating measurable progress in both conference play and overall competition. Overall, the chart suggests that Nebraska is trending upward, becoming more competitive within the Big Ten and more capable of producing postseason-caliber seasons.

title: The effect of the MLB pitch clock
text:
The introduction of the MLB pitch clock was perhaps the most drastic and immediate rule change baseball has seen in decades. The rule took effect after the 2022 season, with 2023 marking the first season under the new timing. The clock fundamentally altered the game’s famously slow cadence. Players, long accustomed to leisurely pacing and endless adjustments on the mound, were forced into constant motion, transforming a sport once defined by patience into one defined by urgency. The single device, ticking down the seconds, accomplished what years of debate could not. The goal: speed up the game and keep fans’ attention. But someone had to benefit from the rule change. Did the batter or the pitcher gain more?
To measure changes in offensive efficiency, I examined yearly OPS, OBP and SLG percentages for the three seasons before and the three seasons after the rule was implemented. These statistics help show whether hitters gained an advantage under the new system.


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

MLB <- read_csv("data/MLB.csv")

obp <- MLB |> 
  filter(Year >= 2020 & Year <= 2025) |> 
  select(Year, OBP)

slg <- MLB |> 
  filter(Year >= 2020 & Year <= 2025) |> 
  select(Year, SLG)

ops <- MLB |> 
  filter(Year >= 2020 & Year <= 2025) |> 
  select(Year, OPS)

MLB_stats <- MLB |> 
  filter(Year >= 2020 & Year <= 2025) |> 
  select(Year, OBP, SLG, OPS) |> 
  pivot_longer(cols = c(OBP, SLG, OPS),
               names_to = "Statistic",
               values_to = "Value")

ggplot(MLB_stats, aes(x = factor(Year), y = Value, fill = Statistic)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("navyblue", "lightgrey", "red")) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 0.8, 0.1),  
    limits = c(0, 0.8)
  )+
  labs(
    title = "Offensive Production Holds Steady Despite the Pitch Clock",
    subtitle= "The pitch clock may have changed timing, but not results at the plate",
    caption = "By:Alex Zetterman | Source: Baseball Reference",
    x = "Season",
    y = "percentages",
    fill = "Statistic"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.caption = element_text(size=10, hjust = 0),
    legend.position = "top"
  )









At first glance, the pitch clock doesn’t appear to have shaken up offensive production. League-wide OPS, OBP and SLG have remained steady from 2020 through 2025, suggesting hitters aren’t necessarily getting on base more or hitting for more power. But stats like OPS, OBP and SLG tell only part of the story. The pitch clock didn’t necessarily change how much offense occurred; it changed how teams generated it.
To better understand whether hitters were rushing their swings or putting more balls in play, analysts can look at the Contact Efficiency Ratio, which measures the number of balls in play for every strikeout. The metric shows whether the faster tempo led to more action or simply more whiffs.


Code
contact_eff <- MLB |>
  filter(Year >= 2020 & Year <= 2025) |>
  group_by(Year) |>
  summarise(
    Total_BIP = sum(BIP, na.rm = TRUE),
    Total_SO = sum(SO, na.rm = TRUE),
    Contact_Efficiency = Total_BIP / Total_SO
  )

# Line chart
ggplot(contact_eff, aes(x = Year, y = Contact_Efficiency)) +
  geom_line(color = "lightblue", size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(color = "black", size = 2.5) +
  
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2023, linetype = "dashed", color = "red", size = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = 2023.1, y = max(contact_eff$Contact_Efficiency, na.rm = TRUE),
           label = "Pitch Clock Introduced (2023)",
           hjust = 0, vjust = 1, color = "red", size = 3, fontface = "italic") +
  
  labs(
    title = "After a 2023 Dip, Contact Rates Begin to Recover",
    subtitle = "Year-to-year changes in BIP/SO indicate gradual adaptation to pitch clock conditions",
    caption = "By:Alex Zetterman | Source: Baseball Reference",
    x = "Season",
    y = "Balls in play per strikeout",

  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size= 15),
    plot.caption = element_text(size=10, hjust = 0),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )









When the pitch clock was first introduced in 2023, contact efficiency took an immediate dip, suggesting hitters initially struggled to adjust to the faster tempo. The sudden pace may have led to more rushed swings and fewer quality at-bats early on. However, from 2023 to 2025, the league’s Contact Efficiency Ratio climbed from about 2.82 to 2.92, showing that hitters quickly adapted to the new rhythm. The rebound suggests that while pitchers gained an early advantage from the rule change, batters have since found their timing again, resulting in more balls in play and a return to offensive balance.
After examining how hitters adjusted, it is equally important to see how pitchers responded to the faster pace. One clear way to do this is by comparing how often pitchers threw strikes versus balls. Charting strikeouts against walks across seasons can show whether the pitch clock improved pitcher command or forced more rushed, less controlled deliveries.


Code
scatter_data <- MLB |>
  filter(Year >= 2020 & Year <= 2025) |>
  group_by(Year) |>
  summarise(
    BB = sum(BB, na.rm = TRUE),
    SO = sum(SO, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
ggplot(scatter_data, aes(x = BB, y = SO)) +
  geom_point(color = "darkred", size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Year), vjust = +1.3, size = 4) +
  
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(3, 3.4)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(8.3, 8.8)) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Walk and Strikeout Rates Drop in Pitch-Clock Era",
    subtitle = "Faster tempo changes how pitchers and hitters approach each plate appearance",
    caption =  "By:Alex Zetterman | Source: Baseball Reference",
    x = "Walks Per Game",
    y = "Strikeouts Per Game"
  ) +
  
  theme_minimal(base_size = 1) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 11),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11),
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 12),
    axis.title.y = element_text(size = 12),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    plot.caption = element_text(size=10, hjust = 0)
  )









The scatter plot shows a clear shift after the pitch clock was introduced: both walks and strikeouts declined in the seasons that followed. Besides in 2023 when walks and strikeouts increased after the pitch-clock was introduced, so it took a year for the pitchers to get used to the change. But, for 2024 and 2025 T pitchers were working faster and relying less on deep, extended counts. The pitch clock allowed fewer walks, fewer strikeouts, and more balls put in play. This trend suggests that the pitch clock didn’t just change the pace of the game; it reshaped how pitchers approached hitters.
Overall, the data suggest that batters initially struggled when the pitch clock was introduced in 2023. Contact Efficiency dipped as hitters rushed their swings, leading to fewer quality at-bats. However, by 2025, hitters had adjusted, and BIP per strikeout rebounded, showing that batters regained their timing and were able to generate offense at similar levels as before. League-wide OPS, OBP, and SLG remained largely steady from 2020 to 2025, indicating that overall offensive production did not dramatically change, even with the faster pace.
On the pitcher side, the scatter plot shows that both walks and strikeouts decreased after the rule change, suggesting pitchers worked faster and relied less on long at-bats. While they may have gained an early advantage in 2023, by 2024–2025 their command stabilized, and the pace of the game created more balls in play rather than extreme outcomes. Taken together, this evidence indicates that hitters ultimately adapted faster, while pitchers saw only temporary gains. Therefore, while both sides felt the impact of the pitch clock, batters appear to have benefited more in the long run by adjusting successfully to the new tempo.
As every coach says, you can’t score unless you put the ball in play, and that’s exactly what batters are doing more consistently since the pitch clock change.
